about: Probability and Statistics (BUSI40002) is a core 7.5 ECTS module in the Autumn term of Year 1 of Imperial Business School's BSc Economics, Finance and Data Science; under Imperial's regulations a core module must be passed and cannot be compensated. Imperial publishes no syllabus or module descriptor, so the topics here are not an official list: a first-year student's post on the Business School blog (March 2025) says only that it moves from probability theory into statistics, so the topics here follow the standard first-year path from probability to inference that later econometrics and machine-learning modules build on; check them against your lecture schedule. The programme specification says assessment mixes coursework (such as problem sets) with examinations, with unseen exams carrying most weight in most modules, but gives no breakdown for this module.
topics: Probability foundations: sample spaces, axioms and counting
Conditional probability, independence and Bayes' theorem
Discrete random variables: expectation, variance, binomial and Poisson
Continuous random variables and the normal distribution
Sampling distributions, the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem
Point estimation: unbiasedness, efficiency and maximum likelihood

notes.h: Probability foundations: sample spaces, axioms and counting
notes.body:
Probability is the language for uncertainty in finance (returns), economics (shocks) and data science (noise in data). Everything starts from a precise set-up.

Basic objects
- An experiment produces one outcome. The sample space Ω is the set of all possible outcomes.
- An event is a subset of Ω. Events combine with set operations: A ∪ B ("A or B"), A ∩ B ("A and B"), Aᶜ ("not A").
- A and B are mutually exclusive (disjoint) if A ∩ B = ∅.

Kolmogorov's axioms
- P(A) ≥ 0 for every event A.
- P(Ω) = 1.
- If A₁, A₂, … are pairwise disjoint, P(A₁ ∪ A₂ ∪ …) = P(A₁) + P(A₂) + …

Consequences you should be able to prove from the axioms
- P(Aᶜ) = 1 − P(A), so P(∅) = 0.
- If A ⊆ B then P(A) ≤ P(B).
- Addition rule: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B).
- Example: if 30% of firms export, 20% import and 10% do both, then P(export or import) = 0.3 + 0.2 − 0.1 = 0.4.

Equally likely outcomes
- If Ω is finite and every outcome is equally likely, P(A) = |A|/|Ω|.
- Two fair dice: 36 outcomes; a total of 7 arises in 6 ways, so P = 6/36 = 1/6.

Counting rules
- Multiplication principle: k stages with n₁, n₂, … choices give n₁ × n₂ × … outcomes.
- Ordered selections without replacement (permutations): nPr = n!/(n − r)!. Choosing a chair, deputy and secretary from 10 people: 10 × 9 × 8 = 720.
- Unordered selections (combinations): nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!). A committee of 3 from 10: 120. Note 720/3! = 120.
- With replacement and order mattering: nʳ (e.g. 2⁴ = 16 head/tail sequences of length 4).
- Example: P(exactly 2 heads in 4 fair tosses) = 4C2/16 = 6/16 = 0.375.
- Five-card poker hands: 52C5 = 2,598,960.

Interpretations
- Frequentist: probability is the long-run relative frequency in repeated trials (made precise by the law of large numbers later in the module).
- Subjective/Bayesian: probability measures a degree of belief, updated with data via Bayes' theorem.

Common pitfalls
- Adding probabilities of events that are not disjoint (double counting the overlap).
- Confusing ordered and unordered counts: ask "does swapping two chosen items give a different outcome?"
- Assuming outcomes are equally likely when they are not (the sums of two dice are not equally likely).

Exam tips: define your events with letters before calculating; write which counting rule you use and why; check that your answer lies between 0 and 1 and that complementary probabilities add to 1.

notes.h: Conditional probability, independence and Bayes' theorem
notes.body:
Information changes probabilities. Conditional probability makes that precise, and Bayes' theorem lets you reverse the direction of conditioning, which is central to classification in data science and to updating beliefs in finance.

Conditional probability
- P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B), for P(B) > 0. It is the probability of A when we know B has happened: B becomes the new sample space.
- Multiplication rule: P(A ∩ B) = P(A | B)P(B) = P(B | A)P(A).
- Chain rule: P(A ∩ B ∩ C) = P(A)P(B | A)P(C | A ∩ B).

Independence
- A and B are independent if P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B), equivalently P(A | B) = P(A).
- Independence is not the same as being mutually exclusive. If A and B are disjoint with positive probabilities, they are dependent: knowing B happened tells you A did not.
- Events A₁, …, Aₙ are mutually independent if the product rule holds for every sub-collection, not just pairs.

Law of total probability
- If B₁, …, Bₖ partition Ω, then P(A) = Σ P(A | Bᵢ)P(Bᵢ).

Bayes' theorem
- P(Bⱼ | A) = P(A | Bⱼ)P(Bⱼ) / Σ P(A | Bᵢ)P(Bᵢ).
- Terms: P(Bⱼ) is the prior, P(A | Bⱼ) the likelihood, P(Bⱼ | A) the posterior.

Worked example (base-rate effect)
- A disease affects 1% of people. A test detects 95% of cases (sensitivity) but also gives a positive result for 5% of healthy people (false positive rate).
- P(+) = 0.95 × 0.01 + 0.05 × 0.99 = 0.0095 + 0.0495 = 0.059.
- P(disease | +) = 0.0095/0.059 ≈ 0.161.
- Only about 16% of positives are true cases, because the condition is rare. Ignoring the prior is called the base-rate fallacy.
- The same logic applies to fraud detection, credit scoring and spam filters: when the event is rare, even an accurate classifier produces many false alarms.

Tree diagrams
- Draw the prior split first, then the conditional branches. Multiply along a path for joint probabilities; add across paths for totals.

Odds form (useful shortcut)
- Posterior odds = prior odds × likelihood ratio. In the example, prior odds 1:99, likelihood ratio 0.95/0.05 = 19, so posterior odds 19:99, giving 19/118 ≈ 0.161.

Common confusions
- P(A | B) ≠ P(B | A) in general (the "prosecutor's fallacy").
- Pairwise independence does not imply mutual independence.

Exam tips: write down the partition and every given probability as a conditional statement before calculating; show the denominator from the law of total probability explicitly; give a one-line interpretation of the posterior.

notes.h: Discrete random variables: expectation, variance, binomial and Poisson
notes.body:
A random variable X is a function that assigns a number to each outcome. It is discrete if it takes a countable set of values.

Probability mass function (pmf) and cdf
- p(x) = P(X = x), with p(x) ≥ 0 and Σ p(x) = 1.
- Cumulative distribution function F(x) = P(X ≤ x): non-decreasing, from 0 to 1, a step function for discrete X.

Expectation and variance
- E[X] = Σ x p(x): the probability-weighted average (long-run mean).
- E[g(X)] = Σ g(x)p(x). In general E[g(X)] ≠ g(E[X]) unless g is linear.
- Linearity: E[aX + b] = aE[X] + b, and E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y] always (no independence needed).
- Var(X) = E[(X − μ)²] = E[X²] − (E[X])². Standard deviation σ = √Var(X).
- Var(aX + b) = a²Var(X): shifting does not change spread; scaling by a multiplies the variance by a².

Worked example
- A bet pays £10 with probability 0.2, £0 with 0.5 and −£5 with 0.3.
- E[X] = 2 + 0 − 1.5 = £0.50. E[X²] = 100(0.2) + 25(0.3) = 27.5. Var(X) = 27.5 − 0.25 = 27.25, so σ ≈ £5.22.

Bernoulli and binomial
- Bernoulli(p): X = 1 with probability p, 0 otherwise. E = p, Var = p(1 − p).
- Binomial(n, p): number of successes in n independent trials with the same p. P(X = k) = nCk pᵏ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ. E = np, Var = np(1 − p).
- Example: n = 10, p = 0.3. P(X = 2) = 45 × 0.09 × 0.7⁸ ≈ 0.2335. Mean 3, variance 2.1.
- Conditions to check: fixed n, two outcomes, constant p, independence.

Poisson
- Counts of events in a fixed interval when events occur independently at a constant average rate λ.
- P(X = k) = e^(−λ)λᵏ/k!, for k = 0, 1, 2, … E = Var = λ.
- Example: claims arrive at 2 per day. P(no claims) = e^(−2) ≈ 0.135; P(3 claims) = e^(−2)·8/6 ≈ 0.180.
- Approximation: Binomial(n, p) ≈ Poisson(np) when n is large and p small.

Geometric
- Number of trials until the first success: P(X = k) = (1 − p)^(k−1)p, E = 1/p.

Why it matters: expected value and variance are the first two building blocks of mean–variance portfolio theory; binomial trees price options; Poisson counts model defaults, trades and website arrivals.

Exam tips: always state the distribution and its parameters before computing ("X ~ Bin(10, 0.3) because…"); use the complement for "at least" questions; use Var = E[X²] − μ² and keep the units clear.

notes.h: Continuous random variables and the normal distribution
notes.body:
Many quantities (returns, prices, times, heights) are best modelled as continuous. Probabilities then come from areas under a density curve.

Density and distribution functions
- A probability density function (pdf) f(x) ≥ 0 with ∫ f(x) dx = 1 over the whole real line.
- P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx. Any single point has probability zero, so ≤ and < give the same answers.
- The cdf F(x) = P(X ≤ x) = ∫ from −∞ to x of f(t) dt, and f(x) = F′(x).
- E[X] = ∫ x f(x) dx and Var(X) = ∫ x² f(x) dx − μ².
- f(x) is not a probability and can exceed 1 (e.g. Uniform(0, 0.5) has density 2).

Uniform(a, b)
- f(x) = 1/(b − a) on [a, b]. Mean (a + b)/2, variance (b − a)²/12.

Exponential(λ)
- f(x) = λe^(−λx) for x ≥ 0. F(x) = 1 − e^(−λx). Mean 1/λ, variance 1/λ².
- Models waiting times between Poisson events. Memoryless: P(X > s + t | X > s) = P(X > t).
- Example: if the mean wait is 2 minutes (λ = 0.5), P(wait > 2) = e^(−1) ≈ 0.368.

Normal N(μ, σ²)
- Bell-shaped and symmetric about μ; f(x) = (1/(σ√(2π))) exp(−(x − μ)²/(2σ²)).
- Standardise: Z = (X − μ)/σ ~ N(0, 1). Use Φ(z) = P(Z ≤ z) from tables or software.
- Rules of thumb: about 68% within 1σ, 95% within 2σ (exactly 1.96σ), 99.7% within 3σ.
- Key quantiles: Φ(1.645) ≈ 0.95, Φ(1.96) ≈ 0.975, Φ(2.576) ≈ 0.995.
- Linear functions of normals are normal: if X ~ N(μ, σ²) then aX + b ~ N(aμ + b, a²σ²). Sums of independent normals are normal.

Worked example
- IQ-style scores X ~ N(100, 15²). P(X > 130) = P(Z > 2) = 1 − Φ(2) ≈ 0.0228.
- The score exceeded by only 5% of people: 100 + 1.645 × 15 ≈ 124.7.

Finance application: Value at Risk
- If daily portfolio returns are N(0.05%, 1.2%²), the 5% one-day VaR is the loss level exceeded with 5% probability: 0.05% − 1.645 × 1.2% ≈ −1.92%, so a loss of about 1.92%.
- Real returns have fatter tails than the normal, so normal VaR tends to understate extreme losses.

Other distributions you will meet later: the t, χ² and F distributions, which arise from samples of normal data and are used in inference.

Exam tips: sketch the normal curve and shade the region before using tables; use symmetry Φ(−z) = 1 − Φ(z); for inverse questions (find x given a probability) find z first, then x = μ + zσ.

Most interesting questions involve more than one variable: the returns of two assets, income and spending, inflation and unemployment. Joint distributions describe how variables move together.

Joint, marginal and conditional distributions
- Discrete: joint pmf p(x, y) = P(X = x, Y = y). Marginal p_X(x) = Σ over y of p(x, y).
- Continuous: joint density f(x, y), with marginal f_X(x) = ∫ f(x, y) dy.
- Conditional: p(y | x) = p(x, y)/p_X(x).
- X and Y are independent if p(x, y) = p_X(x)p_Y(y) for all x, y.

Conditional expectation
- E[Y | X = x] = Σ y p(y | x). Regression (in econometrics later) models exactly this.
- Law of iterated expectations: E[Y] = E[E[Y | X]].

Covariance
- Cov(X, Y) = E[(X − μ_X)(Y − μ_Y)] = E[XY] − E[X]E[Y].
- Positive if X and Y tend to be above their means together; negative if one tends to be high when the other is low.
- Cov(X, X) = Var(X); Cov(aX + b, cY + d) = ac Cov(X, Y).

Correlation
- ρ = Cov(X, Y)/(σ_X σ_Y), always between −1 and 1.
- ρ = ±1 exactly when Y is a linear function of X. Unaffected by changes of units (apart from sign).
- Correlation measures linear association only.

Independence vs zero correlation
- Independent ⇒ Cov = 0.
- Cov = 0 does not imply independence. Example: X uniform on {−1, 0, 1} and Y = X². Then E[XY] = E[X³] = 0 and E[X] = 0, so Cov = 0, yet Y is completely determined by X.
- (For jointly normal variables, zero correlation does imply independence.)

Linear combinations
- E[aX + bY] = aE[X] + bE[Y].
- Var(aX + bY) = a²Var(X) + b²Var(Y) + 2ab Cov(X, Y).
- If X and Y are independent the covariance term vanishes.

Portfolio example (diversification)
- Two assets with σ₁ = 20%, σ₂ = 30%, correlation 0.25, held 50/50.
- Var = 0.25(0.04) + 0.25(0.09) + 2(0.5)(0.5)(0.25)(0.2)(0.3) = 0.01 + 0.0225 + 0.0075 = 0.04.
- Portfolio σ = 20%, the same as the safer asset alone, even though half the money is in the riskier asset, while the expected return is the average of the two. The lower the correlation, the bigger the risk reduction.

Sample versions
- Sample covariance s_xy = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ)/(n − 1); sample correlation r = s_xy/(s_x s_y).
- Correlation does not mean causation: a third variable or reverse causality may drive the pattern.

Exam tips: always include the 2ab Cov term when finding the variance of a sum; check ρ lies in [−1, 1] as a quick sanity test; give a counterexample like Y = X² when asked whether zero correlation implies independence.

notes.h: Sampling distributions, the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem
notes.body:
Statistics uses a sample to learn about a population. Because the sample is random, any statistic computed from it (like the sample mean) is itself a random variable with its own distribution: the sampling distribution.

Random samples
- X₁, …, Xₙ are a random sample if they are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) with mean μ and variance σ².
- Sample mean X̄ = (X₁ + … + Xₙ)/n.

Mean and variance of X̄
- E[X̄] = μ (by linearity).
- Var(X̄) = σ²/n (independence removes the covariance terms; the 1/n² factor and n terms give σ²/n).
- The standard error SE = σ/√n. To halve the SE you need four times as many observations.

Law of large numbers (LLN)
- As n → ∞, X̄ converges to μ (in probability): the chance that X̄ differs from μ by more than any fixed amount goes to zero.
- Chebyshev's inequality gives a quick proof: P(|X̄ − μ| ≥ k) ≤ Var(X̄)/k² = σ²/(nk²) → 0.
- Justifies the frequentist interpretation and Monte Carlo simulation: averages of many simulated draws approximate expectations.

Central limit theorem (CLT)
- For i.i.d. data with finite variance, (X̄ − μ)/(σ/√n) is approximately N(0, 1) for large n, whatever the shape of the original distribution.
- Equivalently, the sum Sₙ = X₁ + … + Xₙ is approximately N(nμ, nσ²).
- Rule of thumb n ≥ 30, but more is needed for very skewed data. If the data are normal, X̄ is exactly normal for any n.

Worked example
- Transaction sizes have μ = £50 and σ = £12. For a sample of n = 36, SE = 12/6 = 2.
- P(X̄ > 53) ≈ P(Z > 1.5) = 1 − Φ(1.5) ≈ 0.067.

Normal approximation to the binomial
- X ~ Bin(n, p) is a sum of n Bernoullis, so X ≈ N(np, np(1 − p)) when np and n(1 − p) are both reasonably large (often ≥ 5 or 10).
- The sample proportion p̂ = X/n ≈ N(p, p(1 − p)/n).
- A continuity correction (e.g. P(X ≤ 20) ≈ P(Y ≤ 20.5)) improves accuracy.

Other sampling distributions (for normal data)
- (n − 1)S²/σ² ~ χ² with n − 1 degrees of freedom, where S² is the sample variance.
- (X̄ − μ)/(S/√n) ~ t with n − 1 degrees of freedom. The t has fatter tails than N(0, 1) and approaches it as n grows.

Simulation view (useful for data science)
- Draw many samples on a computer, compute X̄ each time and plot a histogram: it centres on μ, its spread shrinks like 1/√n and it looks normal even for skewed populations.

Exam tips: distinguish σ (spread of individual data) from σ/√n (spread of the sample mean); state "by the CLT, approximately" when using normality for non-normal data; check np and n(1 − p) before approximating a binomial.

notes.h: Point estimation: unbiasedness, efficiency and maximum likelihood
notes.body:
An estimator is a rule that turns sample data into a guess for an unknown parameter θ (such as a mean μ, a proportion p or a rate λ). The estimate is the number you get from a particular sample.

Properties of estimators
- Bias: Bias(θ̂) = E[θ̂] − θ. Unbiased if E[θ̂] = θ.
- Variance: how much θ̂ varies from sample to sample. Its square root is the standard error.
- Mean squared error: MSE(θ̂) = E[(θ̂ − θ)²] = Var(θ̂) + Bias(θ̂)². A slightly biased estimator can beat an unbiased one on MSE if it has much lower variance (the bias–variance trade-off you will meet again in machine learning).
- Efficiency: among unbiased estimators, prefer the one with the smaller variance.
- Consistency: θ̂ → θ as n → ∞ (e.g. if bias and variance both go to zero).

Standard estimators
- X̄ is unbiased for μ, with variance σ²/n.
- The sample variance S² = Σ(Xᵢ − X̄)²/(n − 1) is unbiased for σ². Dividing by n instead gives an estimator with expectation (n − 1)σ²/n, which is biased downwards, because the deviations are measured from X̄ rather than the true μ.
- The sample proportion p̂ = X/n is unbiased for p, with variance p(1 − p)/n.

Comparing estimators: example
- For μ, compare X̄ with θ̃ = (X₁ + Xₙ)/2. Both are unbiased, but Var(θ̃) = σ²/2 while Var(X̄) = σ²/n, so X̄ is more efficient for n > 2.

Method of moments
- Set sample moments equal to population moments and solve. For an exponential distribution with mean 1/λ, setting X̄ = 1/λ gives λ̂ = 1/X̄.

Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE)
- The likelihood L(θ) = Π f(xᵢ; θ) is the probability (or density) of the observed sample, viewed as a function of θ.
- The MLE maximises L(θ), or equivalently the log-likelihood ℓ(θ) = Σ ln f(xᵢ; θ). Set dℓ/dθ = 0 and check it is a maximum.
- Bernoulli(p): ℓ(p) = (Σxᵢ) ln p + (n − Σxᵢ) ln(1 − p). Setting the derivative to zero gives p̂ = Σxᵢ/n = x̄.
- Poisson(λ): ℓ(λ) = −nλ + (Σxᵢ) ln λ − Σ ln(xᵢ!). Derivative −n + Σxᵢ/λ = 0 gives λ̂ = x̄.
- Exponential(λ): ℓ(λ) = n ln λ − λΣxᵢ, derivative n/λ − Σxᵢ = 0 gives λ̂ = 1/x̄.
- Normal(μ, σ²): μ̂ = x̄ and σ̂² = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)²/n (the MLE of the variance is the biased version).
- Invariance: the MLE of g(θ) is g(θ̂).
- MLEs are generally consistent and, in large samples, approximately normal and efficient. Logistic regression and many machine-learning models are fitted by maximum likelihood.

Exam tips: show the log-likelihood, its derivative and the solution in that order; check the second derivative is negative; when asked about bias, compute E[θ̂] explicitly using linearity.

A point estimate alone hides its uncertainty. A confidence interval (CI) gives a range of plausible values for the parameter, with a stated confidence level.

General form
- Estimate ± critical value × standard error.
- A 95% CI is built by a procedure that captures the true parameter in 95% of repeated samples.
- Correct interpretation: "if we repeated the sampling many times, 95% of intervals constructed this way would contain μ". The true μ is fixed; it is the interval that is random. Avoid saying "there is a 95% probability that μ lies in this particular interval" in a frequentist answer.

CI for a mean, σ known (or n large)
- x̄ ± z_(α/2) σ/√n, with z = 1.645 (90%), 1.96 (95%), 2.576 (99%).
- Example: x̄ = 120, σ = 15, n = 25: SE = 3, 95% CI = 120 ± 5.88 = (114.12, 125.88).

CI for a mean, σ unknown (normal data)
- x̄ ± t_(n−1, α/2) s/√n, using the t distribution with n − 1 degrees of freedom.
- Example: n = 16, x̄ = 52, s = 8. SE = 2 and t₁₅ (0.975) ≈ 2.131. 95% CI = 52 ± 4.26 = (47.74, 56.26).
- t critical values exceed z values (fatter tails), reflecting extra uncertainty from estimating σ; the gap shrinks as n grows.
- For large n the CLT justifies the z interval with s in place of σ even for non-normal data.

CI for a proportion (large n)
- p̂ ± z √(p̂(1 − p̂)/n).
- Example: 160 of 400 surveyed customers would switch bank. p̂ = 0.4, SE = √(0.24/400) ≈ 0.0245, 95% CI ≈ 0.4 ± 0.048 = (0.352, 0.448).

CI for a difference in means (independent large samples)
- (x̄₁ − x̄₂) ± z √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂).

What controls the width?
- Higher confidence ⇒ wider interval.
- More variable data (larger σ) ⇒ wider.
- Larger sample ⇒ narrower, in proportion to 1/√n.

Choosing a sample size
- To estimate μ within ±E with 95% confidence: n ≥ (1.96σ/E)².
- For a proportion with no prior guess use p = 0.5 (the worst case): n ≥ 1.96² × 0.25/E². For E = 0.03 this gives n ≥ 1067.1, so 1,068.

Link to testing
- A 95% CI contains exactly those values μ₀ that a two-sided 5% test would not reject.

Exam tips: always state the formula, the critical value with its degrees of freedom, the SE and the final interval to sensible decimal places; then write a one-sentence interpretation in context; round sample sizes up, never down.

Hypothesis testing asks whether data are consistent with a specific claim about a population. It is used to judge whether a trading strategy beats zero, whether a policy changed an outcome, or whether a model coefficient matters.

The framework
- Null hypothesis H₀: the default claim, usually "no effect" (e.g. μ = μ₀).
- Alternative H₁: what we look for evidence of. Two-sided (μ ≠ μ₀) or one-sided (μ > μ₀ or μ < μ₀), decided before seeing the data.
- Test statistic: measures how far the estimate is from H₀ in standard-error units.
- Significance level α (often 5%): the probability of rejecting H₀ when it is true that we are willing to accept.
- Decision: reject H₀ if the statistic falls in the critical region, or equivalently if the p-value < α.

p-values
- The p-value is the probability, assuming H₀ is true, of getting a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed.
- Small p-value = data would be surprising if H₀ were true.
- It is not the probability that H₀ is true, and a large p-value does not prove H₀; we only "fail to reject" it.

Errors and power
- Type I error: rejecting a true H₀; probability α.
- Type II error: failing to reject a false H₀; probability β.
- Power = 1 − β: the probability of detecting a real effect. Power rises with sample size, effect size and α, and falls with noise σ.
- Lowering α reduces Type I errors but, for fixed n, raises Type II errors.

z-test for a mean (σ known or n large)
- z = (x̄ − μ₀)/(σ/√n). Two-sided 5% critical values ±1.96; one-sided 1.645.

t-test for a mean (σ unknown, normal data)
- t = (x̄ − μ₀)/(s/√n) with n − 1 degrees of freedom.
- Example: H₀: μ = 50 vs H₁: μ ≠ 50, with n = 16, x̄ = 52, s = 8. t = 2/2 = 1. The 5% critical value is 2.131, so we do not reject H₀ (two-sided p ≈ 0.33).

Test for a proportion
- z = (p̂ − p₀)/√(p₀(1 − p₀)/n), using p₀ (the null value) in the standard error.
- Example: a firm claims 30% market share; a sample of 500 finds 130 customers (p̂ = 0.26). z = −0.04/√(0.21/500) ≈ −1.95. Two-sided p ≈ 0.051: just not significant at 5%, though significant one-sided.

Difference in means
- z = (x̄₁ − x̄₂)/√(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂) for large independent samples; a pooled or Welch t-test for small samples.

Good practice
- Statistical significance is not practical importance: with a huge n, tiny effects become "significant".
- Running many tests inflates false positives (multiple testing, "p-hacking"): with 20 independent tests at 5%, about one false rejection is expected even if every null is true.
- Report effect sizes and confidence intervals, not just p-values.

Exam tips: always write H₀ and H₁ in terms of the parameter, state α, give the statistic with its distribution under H₀, then the decision and a conclusion in context ("there is insufficient evidence at the 5% level that…").

cards.b: P(A) ≥ 0; P(Ω) = 1; for pairwise disjoint events, P of the union equals the sum of the probabilities.

Ignoring how rare the condition is. With 1% prevalence, 95% sensitivity and 5% false positives, P(disease | +) is only about 0.16.

E[X] = Σ x·P(X = x).

F(x) = ∫ f(t) dt from −∞ to x, and f(x) = F′(x).

Portfolio variance includes 2w₁w₂ρσ₁σ₂; when ρ < 1 the portfolio SD is below the weighted average of the individual SDs.

cards.b: E[X̄] = μ and Var(X̄) = σ²/n.
σ/√n: the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of X̄.
As n grows, the sample mean X̄ converges (in probability) to the population mean μ.
For i.i.d. data with finite variance, (X̄ − μ)/(σ/√n) is approximately N(0, 1) for large n, whatever the population shape.

The probability, assuming H₀ is true, of a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed.

cards.b: No. It means the data are consistent with H₀ (we fail to reject); the test may simply lack power.
Running many tests at level α makes false positives likely (e.g. about 1 in 20 at 5% when every null is true).

questions.q: In how many ways can a committee of 3 be chosen from 10 people?
questions.why: Order does not matter, so the count is 10C3 = 10!/(3!·7!) = 120. 720 = 10 × 9 × 8 counts ordered selections (e.g. chair, deputy, secretary). 240 divides 10 × 9 × 8 by 3 instead of by 3! = 6, and 1000 = 10³ allows repeats and order.

questions.q: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4 and P(A ∪ B) = 0.7. What is P(A ∩ Bᶜ)?
questions.why: From the addition rule P(A ∩ B) = 0.5 + 0.4 − 0.7 = 0.2, so P(A ∩ Bᶜ) = P(A) − P(A ∩ B) = 0.3. The value 0.2 is P(A ∩ B) itself, 0.5 is P(A), and 0.1 is P(A) − P(B), which would be right only if B were contained in A.

questions.q: A fair coin is tossed 5 times. Find (a) the probability of exactly 3 heads, (b) the probability of at least one head, and (c) explain which counting rules you used.
markScheme: Sample space has 2⁵ = 32 equally likely outcomes.
At least one head via complement: 1 − (1/2)⁵ = 31/32 ≈ 0.969.
Explains 5C3 counts the positions of the heads (unordered choice of positions).
Explains use of the complement rule rather than adding many cases.
questions.modelAnswer: Each toss has 2 outcomes, so by the multiplication principle there are 2⁵ = 32 equally likely sequences. (a) A sequence with exactly 3 heads is fixed by choosing which 3 of the 5 positions are heads; the order of choosing does not matter, so there are 5C3 = 10 such sequences and P = 10/32 = 0.3125. (b) 'At least one head' is the complement of 'no heads', which is the single sequence TTTTT. So P = 1 − 1/32 = 31/32 ≈ 0.969. (c) The multiplication principle gives the size of the sample space, combinations count positions for the heads, and the complement rule avoids adding the cases of 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 heads separately.

questions.q: 4% of borrowers default. A model flags 90% of defaulters and 10% of non-defaulters. What is the probability that a flagged borrower defaults?
questions.why: P(flag) = 0.9 × 0.04 + 0.1 × 0.96 = 0.132, so P(default | flag) = 0.036/0.132 = 3/11 ≈ 0.273. 0.9 is P(flag | default), the reverse conditional. 0.036 is the joint probability P(default and flag), and 0.132 is P(flag) on its own.

questions.q: P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.5, and A and B are independent. What is P(A ∪ B)?
questions.why: Independence gives P(A ∩ B) = 0.3 × 0.5 = 0.15, so P(A ∪ B) = 0.3 + 0.5 − 0.15 = 0.65. 0.8 forgets to subtract the overlap (that would only be right for disjoint events), 0.15 is the intersection, and 0.5 is just P(B).

questions.q: Factory X makes 60% of a product and factory Y makes 40%. 2% of X's output and 5% of Y's output is defective. (a) Find the probability a randomly chosen item is defective. (b) Given an item is defective, find the probability it came from Y. (c) Are 'defective' and 'made by Y' independent? Justify.
markScheme: Shows the joint P(Y ∩ D) = 0.02 explicitly.
Compares P(D | Y) = 0.05 with P(D) = 0.032 (or P(Y | D) with P(Y)).
Concludes not independent, with interpretation (Y's items are more often defective).
questions.modelAnswer: (a) By the law of total probability, P(D) = P(D | X)P(X) + P(D | Y)P(Y) = 0.02 × 0.6 + 0.05 × 0.4 = 0.012 + 0.020 = 0.032. (b) By Bayes, P(Y | D) = P(D | Y)P(Y)/P(D) = 0.020/0.032 = 0.625. So although Y makes only 40% of items, it accounts for 62.5% of defectives. (c) Independence would need P(D | Y) = P(D). But P(D | Y) = 0.05 while P(D) = 0.032; equivalently P(Y | D) = 0.625 ≠ P(Y) = 0.4. So the events are dependent: knowing an item is from Y raises the chance it is defective.

questions.q: X ~ Binomial(10, 0.3). What are E[X] and Var(X)?
questions.why: For a binomial, E[X] = np = 3 and Var(X) = np(1 − p) = 10 × 0.3 × 0.7 = 2.1. 0.21 is p(1 − p), the variance of a single Bernoulli trial. 0.3 is p, not the mean count. Mean equal to variance is a property of the Poisson, not the binomial.

questions.q: Calls arrive at a call centre as a Poisson process with an average of 2 per minute. What is the probability of at least 2 calls in a given minute?

An investment returns +20% with probability 0.5, 0% with probability 0.3 and −30% with probability 0.2. Find the expected return and the standard deviation of the return. If you invest £1,000, what are the mean and standard deviation of your profit in pounds?
questions.modelAnswer: Work in percentage points. E[R] = 0.5 × 20 + 0.3 × 0 + 0.2 × (−30) = 10 − 6 = 4%. E[R²] = 0.5 × 400 + 0.3 × 0 + 0.2 × 900 = 200 + 180 = 380. Var(R) = 380 − 4² = 364, so SD(R) = √364 ≈ 19.08%. With £1,000 invested, profit = £10 × R (since 1% of £1,000 is £10). So E[profit] = 10 × 4 = £40 and SD(profit) = 10 × 19.08 ≈ £190.79, using Var(aX) = a²Var(X), so SD scales by |a|.

questions.why: Standardise: z = (130 − 100)/15 = 2, so P(X > 130) = 1 − Φ(2) ≈ 0.0228. 0.159 is P(Z > 1), the tail beyond one standard deviation rather than two. 0.977 is P(X < 130). 0.05 is the two-tailed probability beyond ±2σ from the 68–95–99.7 rule, not halved to give the single upper tail.

questions.q: Waiting times are exponential with mean 2 minutes. You have already waited 3 minutes. What is the probability you wait at least 2 more minutes?
questions.why: With λ = 0.5 the memoryless property gives P(X > 5 | X > 3) = P(X > 2) = e^(−0.5 × 2) = e^(−1) ≈ 0.368. e^(−2.5) is the unconditional P(X > 5), ignoring the information already gained. 1 − e^(−1) is the probability of waiting less than 2 more minutes. e^(−1.5) is P(X > 3), the time already waited.

questions.q: Daily returns on a portfolio are modelled as N(0.05%, (1.2%)²). (a) Find the probability of a daily loss (return below 0). (b) Find the 5% one-day Value at Risk as a percentage. (c) Give one reason this VaR figure may understate risk.
markScheme: Correct interpretation: a loss bigger than 1.92% is expected on about 1 day in 20.
Limitation: real returns have fat tails (or volatility changes over time), so extreme losses are more likely than the normal predicts.
questions.modelAnswer: (a) z = (0 − 0.05)/1.2 ≈ −0.0417, so P(R < 0) = Φ(−0.0417) ≈ 0.483: a loss on just under half of days. (b) The 5% quantile of R is μ − 1.645σ = 0.05 − 1.645 × 1.2 = 0.05 − 1.974 = −1.924%. So the 5% one-day VaR is a loss of about 1.92% of the portfolio: on roughly 1 day in 20 the loss is expected to exceed this. (c) Actual daily returns have fatter tails than the normal distribution, so very large losses happen more often than the model says; volatility also clusters over time, so a constant σ can understate risk in turbulent periods. VaR also says nothing about how large losses are beyond the threshold.

questions.q: Assets A and B have standard deviations 20% and 30% and correlation 0.25. What is the standard deviation of a 50/50 portfolio?
questions.why: Variance = 0.25 × 0.04 + 0.25 × 0.09 + 2 × 0.5 × 0.5 × 0.25 × 0.2 × 0.3 = 0.04, so SD = 20%. 25% is the simple average of the SDs, which is only right if the correlation is 1. 18.0% (√0.0325) drops the covariance term, which would be right only with zero correlation. 15.8% (√0.025) subtracts the covariance term instead of adding it, as if the correlation were −0.25.

questions.q: Which statement about correlation is true?
options: If X and Y are independent, their correlation is zero.
If the correlation between X and Y is zero, they must be independent.
A correlation of 0.9 shows that X causes Y.
Correlation changes if X is measured in pence instead of pounds.
questions.why: Independence makes E[XY] = E[X]E[Y], so covariance and correlation are zero. The reverse fails: Y = X² with X symmetric about 0 gives zero correlation with full dependence. High correlation does not establish causation. Correlation is unit-free, so rescaling X by 100 leaves it unchanged.

questions.q: X and Y have joint pmf P(0, 0) = 0.2, P(0, 1) = 0.3, P(1, 0) = 0.4, P(1, 1) = 0.1. (a) Find the marginal distributions. (b) Find Cov(X, Y) and the correlation. (c) Are X and Y independent?
questions.modelAnswer: (a) P(X = 0) = 0.2 + 0.3 = 0.5 and P(X = 1) = 0.4 + 0.1 = 0.5; P(Y = 0) = 0.2 + 0.4 = 0.6 and P(Y = 1) = 0.3 + 0.1 = 0.4. (b) E[X] = 0.5, E[Y] = 0.4, and XY = 1 only at (1, 1), so E[XY] = 0.1. Cov(X, Y) = 0.1 − 0.5 × 0.4 = −0.1. Var(X) = 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25 and Var(Y) = 0.4 × 0.6 = 0.24 (Bernoulli variances). ρ = −0.1/√(0.25 × 0.24) = −0.1/0.2449 ≈ −0.408. (c) No: independence would need P(X = 1, Y = 1) = 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.2, but it is 0.1. The non-zero covariance already shows dependence.

questions.q: Transaction values have mean £50 and standard deviation £12. For a random sample of 36 transactions, what is the approximate probability that the sample mean exceeds £53?
questions.why: SE = 12/√36 = 2, so z = (53 − 50)/2 = 1.5 and P(Z > 1.5) ≈ 0.067 by the CLT. 0.401 comes from using σ = 12 instead of the standard error (z = 0.25). 0.933 is P(Z < 1.5). 0.5 would be the probability of exceeding the mean itself.

questions.q: Which statement about the central limit theorem is correct?
options: It says the variance of the sample mean increases with n.
It says the sample mean is approximately normal for large n, even if the population is not normal.
It says that large samples of data are themselves normally distributed.
It requires the population to be normal.
questions.why: The CLT is about the sampling distribution of X̄ (or of a sum), not the data: a large sample from a skewed population is still skewed, but its mean is approximately normal. Normal populations give exact normality for any n, so normality is not required. Var(X̄) = σ²/n falls as n increases.

questions.q: A fair coin is tossed 400 times. Use the normal approximation to find the probability that the number of heads is between 190 and 210 inclusive. State the approximation you use and why it is justified.
markScheme: X ~ Bin(400, 0.5) with mean 200 and variance 100 (SD 10).
Justifies: np = n(1 − p) = 200 are large, so CLT applies.
questions.modelAnswer: Let X be the number of heads, X ~ Bin(400, 0.5). Mean np = 200 and variance np(1 − p) = 100, so SD = 10. Since np = n(1 − p) = 200 are large, X is a sum of 400 i.i.d. Bernoulli variables and the CLT gives X ≈ Y ~ N(200, 10²). With a continuity correction, P(190 ≤ X ≤ 210) ≈ P(189.5 ≤ Y ≤ 210.5) = P(−1.05 ≤ Z ≤ 1.05) = 2Φ(1.05) − 1 ≈ 2(0.8531) − 1 ≈ 0.706. (Without the correction you would get 2Φ(1) − 1 ≈ 0.683; the exact binomial answer is about 0.706.)

questions.q: For an i.i.d. sample from N(μ, σ²), which estimator of σ² is unbiased?
questions.why: Dividing by n − 1 gives E[S²] = σ². Dividing by n is the MLE but has expectation (n − 1)σ²/n, a downward bias; dividing by n + 1 is biased further down. The last expression squares a sum of deviations that is always zero, so it equals 0.

questions.q: A sample of 5 daily counts of trades from a Poisson distribution is 3, 5, 2, 4, 6. What is the maximum likelihood estimate of λ?
questions.why: For the Poisson the MLE is the sample mean: (3 + 5 + 2 + 4 + 6)/5 = 20/5 = 4. 1/4 is the exponential-rate formula 1/x̄, which does not apply to Poisson counts. 20 is the total, not the mean. 2 is the sample variance (10/5 with divisor n), not the MLE.

questions.q: X₁, …, Xₙ are i.i.d. exponential with density f(x) = λe^(−λx), x ≥ 0. (a) Write down the log-likelihood. (b) Derive the MLE of λ and check it is a maximum. (c) Hence state the MLE of the mean 1/λ and say whether it is unbiased.
markScheme: L(λ) = λⁿ exp(−λΣxᵢ); ℓ(λ) = n ln λ − λΣxᵢ.
dℓ/dλ = n/λ − Σxᵢ = 0 gives λ̂ = n/Σxᵢ = 1/x̄.
By invariance the MLE of 1/λ is x̄.
x̄ is unbiased for the mean because E[X̄] = E[X] = 1/λ.
questions.modelAnswer: (a) L(λ) = Π λe^(−λxᵢ) = λⁿ e^(−λΣxᵢ), so ℓ(λ) = n ln λ − λΣxᵢ. (b) dℓ/dλ = n/λ − Σxᵢ. Setting this to zero gives λ̂ = n/Σxᵢ = 1/x̄. The second derivative is −n/λ² < 0 for all λ > 0, so this is a maximum. (c) By the invariance property, the MLE of the mean 1/λ is 1/λ̂ = x̄. It is unbiased because E[X̄] = (1/n)Σ E[Xᵢ] = 1/λ. (Note that λ̂ = 1/x̄ itself is biased, because E[1/X̄] ≠ 1/E[X̄] in general.)

questions.q: A sample of 16 observations from a normal population has mean 52 and standard deviation 8. Which is the 95% confidence interval for μ?
questions.why: σ is unknown, so use t with 15 degrees of freedom: 52 ± 2.131 × 8/4 = 52 ± 4.26. Using z = 1.96 instead of the t value gives (48.08, 55.92), which is too narrow. Forgetting to divide by √n gives 52 ± 1.96 × 8, about (36.32, 67.68). 52 ± 2 is just one standard error with no critical value.

questions.q: A researcher reports a 95% confidence interval for mean weekly spending of (£42, £58). Which interpretation is correct?
options: 95% of customers spend between £42 and £58 a week.
There is a 95% chance that the sample mean lies between £42 and £58.
The true mean is £50 with 95% certainty.
If the study were repeated many times, about 95% of intervals built this way would contain the true mean.
questions.why: Confidence refers to the long-run success rate of the procedure. The interval is about the population mean, not individual customers, so the '95% of customers' reading confuses it with a prediction interval. The sample mean is known (£50, the centre) so there is nothing uncertain about it. The interval does not pin the true mean to £50.

questions.q: In a survey of 400 UK students, 160 say they use a budgeting app. (a) Construct a 95% confidence interval for the population proportion. (b) How large a sample would be needed for a 95% interval of half-width 0.03, with no prior estimate of p?
markScheme: Uses p = 0.5 for the worst case: n ≥ 1.96² × 0.25/0.03².
questions.modelAnswer: (a) p̂ = 160/400 = 0.4. SE = √(0.4 × 0.6/400) = √0.0006 ≈ 0.0245. The 95% margin is 1.96 × 0.0245 ≈ 0.048, so the CI is 0.4 ± 0.048 = (0.352, 0.448). We are 95% confident that between about 35% and 45% of UK students use a budgeting app, in the sense that this procedure captures the true proportion in 95% of samples. (b) Half-width E = 1.96√(p(1 − p)/n). With no prior estimate use p = 0.5, which maximises p(1 − p). Then n ≥ 1.96² × 0.25/0.03² = 0.9604/0.0009 ≈ 1067.1, so at least 1,068 students are needed.

questions.q: A test gives a p-value of 0.03. Which statement is correct?
options: H₀ is rejected at the 5% level but not at the 1% level.
There is a 3% probability that H₀ is true.
H₀ is rejected at both the 5% and 1% levels.
There is a 97% probability that H₁ is true.
questions.why: Reject when p < α: 0.03 < 0.05 but 0.03 > 0.01. A p-value is computed assuming H₀ is true, so it is not the probability that H₀ is true, nor does 1 − p give the probability of H₁. It is not small enough for the 1% level.

questions.q: A firm claims a 30% market share. In a random sample of 500 customers, 130 use the firm. Testing H₀: p = 0.3 against H₁: p ≠ 0.3, what is the approximate z statistic?
questions.why: p̂ = 0.26 and under H₀ the SE is √(0.3 × 0.7/500) ≈ 0.0205, so z = −0.04/0.0205 ≈ −1.95. Using p̂ in the SE (√(0.26 × 0.74/500) ≈ 0.0196) gives about −2.04, which is the confidence-interval SE, not the test SE. −0.04 is the raw difference without standardising. −1.645 is a one-sided critical value, not the statistic.

questions.q: A fund manager claims a strategy earns a positive mean monthly excess return. Over 36 months the mean excess return is 0.6% with sample standard deviation 1.8%. Test H₀: μ = 0 against H₁: μ > 0 at the 5% level. Explain what a Type I error would mean here.
markScheme: States H₀: μ = 0 and H₁: μ > 0 (one-sided), α = 0.05.
Critical value t₃₅ (0.95) ≈ 1.69 (or z = 1.645 for large n).
Type I error: concluding the strategy has a positive mean excess return when in truth it does not.
questions.modelAnswer: H₀: μ = 0, H₁: μ > 0, one-sided at α = 0.05. SE = s/√n = 1.8/6 = 0.3, so t = (0.6 − 0)/0.3 = 2.0, with 35 degrees of freedom under H₀. The one-sided 5% critical value of t₃₅ is about 1.69 (1.645 for the normal approximation). Since 2.0 > 1.69 we reject H₀; the one-sided p-value is about 0.027. There is evidence at the 5% level that the strategy's mean monthly excess return is positive. A Type I error here would be concluding the strategy beats zero when its true mean excess return is actually zero, for example being fooled by a lucky run of months; this happens with probability 5% under H₀.

questions.q:
A bank uses a model to flag loan applicants as high risk. 4% of applicants eventually default. The model flags 90% of applicants who go on to default and 10% of those who do not.
(a) Find the probability that a randomly chosen applicant is flagged. [3 marks]
(b) Find the probability that a flagged applicant defaults. Comment on the result. [5 marks]
(c) The bank lends to 20 flagged applicants, whose outcomes are independent. Let X be the number who default. State the distribution of X and find E[X], Var(X) and P(X = 0). [7 marks]
(d) Each default costs the bank £10,000. Find the mean and standard deviation of the total default loss on these 20 loans. [5 marks]
markScheme: (b) Comment on base rates: most flagged applicants do not default because defaults are rare; false positives dominate.
(c) X ~ Bin(20, 3/11), justified by fixed n, independence and constant p.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Let D = default and F = flagged. P(F) = P(F | D)P(D) + P(F | Dᶜ)P(Dᶜ) = 0.9 × 0.04 + 0.1 × 0.96 = 0.036 + 0.096 = 0.132.

(b) By Bayes' theorem, P(D | F) = P(F | D)P(D)/P(F) = 0.036/0.132 = 3/11 ≈ 0.273. So only about 27% of flagged applicants default, even though the model catches 90% of defaulters. Because defaults are rare (4%), the 10% false-positive rate applied to the large non-defaulting group (96%) produces more flags (0.096) than true defaulters do (0.036). This is the base-rate effect; the flag still raises the default probability from 4% to about 27%, so it is informative.

(c) There are a fixed 20 independent loans, each of which defaults or not, with the same probability p = 3/11. So X ~ Bin(20, 3/11). E[X] = np = 60/11 ≈ 5.45. Var(X) = np(1 − p) = 20 × (3/11) × (8/11) = 480/121 ≈ 3.97 (SD ≈ 1.99). P(X = 0) = (1 − p)²⁰ = (8/11)²⁰ ≈ 0.0017, so it is almost certain that at least one flagged borrower defaults.

(d) Total loss L = 10,000X. By linearity E[L] = 10,000 × 60/11 ≈ £54,545. Var(L) = 10,000² Var(X), so SD(L) = 10,000 × √(480/121) ≈ 10,000 × 1.992 ≈ £19,917. The independence assumption matters: in a recession defaults are positively correlated, which would leave the mean unchanged but make the variance (and the risk of a very large loss) larger.

questions.q:
Waiting times (in minutes) for a customer-service chat are modelled as i.i.d. exponential with rate λ, so the mean wait is θ = 1/λ. A random sample of n = 50 waits has sample mean x̄ = 4.
(a) Derive the maximum likelihood estimator of λ and give the estimate. [6 marks]
(b) Show that X̄ is an unbiased estimator of θ and find its variance in terms of θ. [4 marks]
(c) Using the central limit theorem, construct an approximate 95% confidence interval for θ. [6 marks]
(d) The company claims the mean wait is 5 minutes. Test H₀: θ = 5 against H₁: θ < 5 at the 5% level, stating the p-value. [6 marks]
(e) Explain why the same data might lead to rejecting H₀ if n had been 200. [3 marks]
markScheme: (a) ℓ(λ) = n ln λ − λΣxᵢ; derivative n/λ − Σxᵢ = 0 so λ̂ = 1/x̄ = 0.25 per minute; second derivative −n/λ² < 0.
(b) E[X̄] = θ by linearity; Var(X̄) = θ²/n, using Var(X) = 1/λ² = θ².
(d) One-sided p ≈ 0.079 > 0.05 (critical value −1.645): do not reject H₀; conclusion in context.
(d) Notes consistency with (c): 5 lies inside the interval.
(e) With n = 200 the SE halves to about 0.354, z ≈ −2.83, p ≈ 0.002: more power to detect the same difference.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The likelihood is L(λ) = Π λe^(−λxᵢ) = λⁿe^(−λΣxᵢ), so ℓ(λ) = n ln λ − λΣxᵢ. Then dℓ/dλ = n/λ − Σxᵢ = 0 gives λ̂ = n/Σxᵢ = 1/x̄. Since d²ℓ/dλ² = −n/λ² < 0 this is a maximum. With x̄ = 4, λ̂ = 0.25 per minute. By invariance the MLE of θ = 1/λ is x̄ = 4 minutes.

(b) E[X̄] = (1/n)Σ E[Xᵢ] = (1/n)(nθ) = θ, so X̄ is unbiased for θ. For an exponential, Var(X) = 1/λ² = θ², so by independence Var(X̄) = θ²/n.

(c) By the CLT, X̄ ≈ N(θ, θ²/n) for n = 50. Estimating θ by x̄ in the standard error gives SE ≈ 4/√50 ≈ 0.566. An approximate 95% CI is 4 ± 1.96 × 0.566 = 4 ± 1.109, i.e. (2.89, 5.11) minutes.

(d) H₀: θ = 5 against H₁: θ < 5. Under H₀ the standard deviation of X̄ is θ₀/√n = 5/√50 ≈ 0.707 (for the exponential the SD equals the mean, so the null value fixes it). z = (4 − 5)/0.707 ≈ −1.41. The one-sided p-value is Φ(−1.41) ≈ 0.079. Since 0.079 > 0.05 (equivalently −1.41 > −1.645), we do not reject H₀: there is insufficient evidence at the 5% level that the mean wait is below 5 minutes. This matches (c), where 5 lies just inside the interval (the two procedures use slightly different SEs, so they need not agree exactly).

(e) The standard error shrinks like 1/√n. With n = 200 the null SE would be 5/√200 ≈ 0.354, giving z = −1/0.354 ≈ −2.83 and a p-value of about 0.002, so H₀ would be rejected. The observed difference of 1 minute is the same; a larger sample gives the test more power to tell it apart from sampling noise.
